messages.subject_clean: higher order CFA help.
messages.body_plain:
> #Hierarchical Model 1
> model.h <-  'LV1 =~ Q65+Q55+Q74+Q58+Q62+Q86+Q61+Q56+Q43+Q66+Q12+Q46+Q50+Q71+Q48+Q82+Q63+Q59+Q73+Q53
>              LV2 =~ Q17+Q77+Q21+Q18+Q84+Q19+Q78+Q20+Q79+Q42+Q6+Q85+Q67+Q52
>
>             #Modification index
>             Q55 ~~ Q74
>
>             finIQ =~ NA*LV1 + LV2
>
>             # constrain the variance of finIQ to 1
>             finIQ ~~ 1*finIQ
>
>             '

I'm surprised you didn't get a warning or error.  This model is not identified.  You have 2 latent variances (LV1 and LV2) and a latent correlation, and your higher-order structure is trying to estimate 4 unknowns (2 "loadings" and 2 residual latent variances) from those 3 pieces of information.  Like identifying first-order constructs with only 2 indicators, you should fix both loadings to 1 and estimate the variance, or constrain the loadings to equality and fix the variance to 1.  (Those constraints aren't necessary if the factors correlate with other factors, but your 2nd-order factor doesn't have anything other factors to correlate with.)  I'm in favor of fixing both loadings to 1, because the 2nd-order latent variance is the same estimate as the latent covariance in a first-order CFA -- that makes it even more obvious that the 2nd-order model is equivalent to a first-order CFA, no value added.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Multiple group analyses with Likert items: some different results
messages.body_plain:
loadfit and mIC[["fit.loadings"]] have the same df, but I'm not sure that they are equivalent models (if they were, the chi-squared would be the same).  You say you read through Sunthud's lavaan scripts at the link you provided -- paying attention to those equality constraints tells you exactly how those models (and therefore, the output of measurementInvarianceCat) differ from the models you fit when you use the group.equal argument.  Your lavaan model syntax places no constraints on the thresholds whatsoever, whereas the method Sunthud (based on Millsap & Yun-Tein, 2004) does place equality constraints on the first threshold of each indicator, as well as the second threshold of the first indicator of each construct (i.e., u1 and u5) -- even in the configural model.  This enables the estimation not only of factor means in the second group, but also residual variances of each indicator's underlying latent response in the second group.  When you specify group.equal = "loadings", you did not freely estimate the residual variances, so your model-implied covariance matrix was different than the one implied by the model using semTools -- you can compare them directly:

> lavInspect(loadfit, "cov.ov")
> lavInspect(mIC[["fit.loadings"]], "cov.ov")

This is what makes categorical CFA so much less intuitive than CFA with continuous indicators.  The thresholds affect not only mean-structure parameters but also covariance structure parameters.  For example
If an indicator's latent response has a higher mean in group 2, that would manifest as a negative shift in the thresholds, but I think the distance between thresholds would stay the same (or proportionally equal, if the variances differed)
If an indicator's latent response has a higher variance in group 2, that would manifest as a change in the distance between thresholds
If you only have 1 threshold (binary indicator), then you cannot disentangle group-differences in means from group-differences in variances -- both would manifest as a difference in thresholds.  That is why you can't test weak and strong invariance separately with binary indicators.

Anyway, the reason you have the same df using the 2 methods is that the 8 freely estimated residual variances are compensated by the 8 equality constraints on the first thresholds, and the 2 free factor means in group 2 are compensated by the 2 additional equality constraints on the second thresholds of u1 and u5.  So the number of estimated parameters is the same, but the models are not equivalent.

And this is not a case of one method being wrong whereas the other is correct.  They are just 2 different methods, so you just need to pick one.  The Millsap & Yun-Tein (2004) method has more theoretical support because their publication was very thorough, but the point of their article was to delineate minimum identification constraints while being able to compare latent means and variances (the whole point of testing invariance).  They did not set out to make an exhaustive list of all possible ways to test measurement invariance with categorical indicators.

Terry

messages.subject: Simulate data from LGC factors regressed on observed variables with interaction
messages.subject_clean: Simulate data from LGC factors regressed on observed variables with interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm conducting a power analysis and want to use `simulateData` to generate data from a latent growth curve model where both the intercept and slope are regressed on two observed variables and their interaction. However, I'm finding it difficult to figure out how to generate the data for the interaction term. I know lavaan doesn't support syntax to specify an interaction, so perhaps there are some constraints I can impose that will simulate the proper relationship between the variables such that I can manually compute the interaction term for the model-fitting portion of the power analysis procedure. Or perhaps it's not important that the simulated data encode the multiplication of the two variables as that doesn't affect the covariance matrix?

My code is something like this:

theDGM <- '
i_hrb =~ 1*hrb1 + 1*hrb2 + 1*hrb3 + 1*hrb4
s_hrb =~ 0*hrb1 + .1*hrb2 + .2*hrb3 + .3*hrb4

i_hrb ~ 0*1
s_hrb ~ .5*1

i_hrb ~ .3*A1 + -.2*A2 + .1*A1xA2

i_hrb ~~ -.1*s_hrb'

someData <- simulateData(model=theDGM,
model.type='growth',
standardized=T,
sample.nobs=500)

Using 'empircial=T' in the simulateData call seems to reproduce this model's path weights, but of course A1xA2 != A1 * A2 necessarily.

I'm pretty new at this, so any feedback is appreciated.

(Only tangentially related: please let me know if there is anything wrong with using standardize=T in this way; I'm trying to simulate standardized relations).

Many thanks,
~John

messages.body_plain:
This one piqued my interest, so I can't help but post a solution I worked out, although it may seem like more work than it is worth.  I hope it helps.

Interaction / Moderation means the effect (slope) of A1 depends on the level of A2.  You can switch the roles of A2 and A1 without loss of generality -- it just depends how you want to interpret it.  The important point is that this regression equation:

ŷ = β0 + β1A1 + β2A2 + β12(A1)(A2) ​

can be expressed equivalently by factoring out the common term A2:
ŷ = β0 + β1A1 + (β2 + β12A1) × A2

So the slope of A2 is a function of A1 -- specifically, the slope = β2 + β12A1.  You can capitalize on this parameterization to generate subsets of data for one level of A1 iteratively from min(A1) to max(A1) in some number of increments, such that the subsamples add up to N = 500.  For each iteration, you only need to include A2 as a variable in your model syntax, and after data generation you can save the variable A1 as a constant for that subset of data.

Your example specifies the latent-intercept being regressed on A1 and A2 and their interaction (with intercept == 0):

i_hrb = 0 + 0.3(A1) - 0.2(A2) + 0.1(A1)(A2) ​

which can be expressed equivalently as:

i_hrb = 0.3(A1) + [-0.2 + 0.1(A1)] × A2

So, for example, when A1 == 1, then the equation simplies to:

i_hrb = 0.3(1) + [-0.2 + 0.1(1)] × A2 = 0.3 - 0.1(A2)

And when A1 == 2, the equation simplifies to:

i_hrb = 0.3(2) + [-0.2 + 0.1(2)] × A2 = 0.6 - 0(A2) = 0.6

Using paste(), you can loop through the different levels of A1, constructing the model syntax with appropriate values of the intercept and slope for the i_hrb equation.  To keep the illustration simple, I will generate values of A1 uniformly between 1 and 10, with n = 5 at each integer-value of A1, for a total N = 50.  (You can generate n = 50 for each value of A1 to get N = 500, or you can make A1 look more continuous by keeping n = 5 and using 100 more fine-grained cut-points across the range of A1, but you would probably get similar results either way -- most behavioral research relies on ordinal Likert-type data anyway).

> ## function to generate subset of data at fixed level of A1
> getSubsample <- function(A1, N) {
>   library(lavaan)
>   B0 <- 0 + 0.3*A1
>   B1 <- -.2 + .1*A1
>   theDGM <- paste0('i_hrb =~ 1*hrb1 + 1*hrb2 + 1*hrb3 + 1*hrb4

>          s_hrb =~ 0*hrb1 + .1*hrb2 + .2*hrb3 + .3*hrb4

>          s_hrb ~ .5*1
>          i_hrb ~ ', B0, '*1 + ', B1, '*A2
>          i_hrb ~~ -.1*s_hrb')
>   someData <- simulateData(model = theDGM, model.type = 'growth',
>                            standardized = TRUE, sample.nobs = N)
>   someData$A1 <- A1
>   return(someData)
> }
> ## check if it works
> getSubsample(A1 = 2, N = 10)
> ## now apply it to the range of A1 == 1:10 (with small N to illustrate)
> set.seed(123)
> (dataList <- mapply(getSubsample, A1 = 1:10, N = 5, SIMPLIFY = FALSE))
> ## now combine the list of subsamples
> (myData <- do.call(rbind, dataList))

The distribution of the fixed exogenous variables A1 and A2 is not assumed to be normal (or anything else) unless you choose fixed.x = FALSE, so it doesn't really matter how A1 is distributed.  If you really want A1 to be standard normal, then instead of generating subsamples uniformly across the range of A1, you can generate as many values as you would expect in each of those bins.  Basically, you divide the standard normal curve into k segments/bins, calculate the corresponding cumulative probabilities for the bins, and multiply the total sample size by those probabilities to get subsample sizes in each bin.

> nBins <- 10
> (bins <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = nBins + 1))
> (probs <- pnorm(bins))
> (binprobs <- diff(probs)) # length(binprobs) == nBins
> (binsize <- round(binprobs*500))
> sum(binsize)
> (newbins <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = nBins)) # length(newbins) == nBins

Now, you can apply the getSubsample function again, using the highlighted objects as arguments:

> set.seed(123)
> dataList <- mapply(getSubsample, A1 = newbins, N = binsize, SIMPLIFY = FALSE))
> lapply(dataList, head) # check the top of each subsample
> sapply(dataList, nrow) # check the subsample sizes
> myData <- do.call(rbind, dataList) # stack the dataList

> (Only tangentially related: please let me know if there is anything wrong with using standardize=T in this way; I'm trying to simulate standardized relations).

Figuring out how to standardize is pretty tricky when you have interaction terms (whose total variance is a nontrivial function of the joint distribution of A1 and A2).  In my example above, the HRB variables had SDs around 1.4, similar to your example that yields observed variances > 2

> fitted(growth(theDGM))

and a model-implied variance > 1 for the latent intercept

> lavInspect(growth(theDGM), "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

I would strongly suggest setting all population parameters manually in the syntax (especially because it doesn't make sense to standardize the latent growth factors -- you do not expect their means to be zero!).  Try thinking of change in units of the actual variables you will eventually analyze, choosing effect sizes according to what would be meaningful (i.e., a change that would be considered noticeable in real life).  A standardized effect size is just a real effect size scaled by the variability in the data, but that variability can depend on various aspects of the study design (e.g., the (sub)populations of interest, the measurement instruments, etc.).  If you really are agnostic about what a truly (practically) significant effect would look like and what variability to expect in your data, you can always check your average standardized estimates across 10 trial replications, then adjust your population parameters by trial and error until you are in the ballpark you want.  Just a suggestion.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> This is a really clever solution! I'll try it out. Also, your advice regarding standardization is quite helpful. Many thanks! I hope this will be of use to others as well.

You're welcome.  A couple more things occurred to me after I made this post.
I should not have used "standardized = TRUE" in each separate script -- that will lead to different residual variances of endogenous variables in each subsample, so you end up with unintended (and unmodeled) heteroscedasticity.  That's another reason to instead specify all parameters manually in the lavaan model syntax.
I noticed you set your factor loadings for the latent slope to decimal values {0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3} instead of integers {0, 1, 2, 3}.  The mean of the latent slope is the average amount of change per unit of time, which is now outside the scope of observed time in your simulation (because you are simulating time to range only 3 tenths of a time-unit).  Although there is nothing per se wrong with coding time that way in an analysis, it might complicate your choice of mean and variance parameters for the latent slope.
Good luck,

Terry

messages.body_plain:
In case another SEM newbie also runs into this problem, it was solved for me by defining the 1 factor model the same as the 2 factor model, with the addition of fixing the covariance between the reactive and proactive factor to 1, like so:

RPQ1factor.model <- 'reactive =~ RPQ1 + RPQ3 + RPQ5 + RPQ7 + RPQ8 + RPQ11 + RPQ13 + RPQ14 + RPQ16 + RPQ19 + RPQ22

                               proactive =~ RPQ2 + RPQ4 + RPQ6 + RPQ9 + RPQ10 + RPQ12 + RPQ15 + RPQ17 + RPQ18 + RPQ20 + RPQ21 + RPQ23

                               reactive ~~ 1*proactive'

This is effectively the same as the previous definition of the 1 factor model, but it makes it possible for Lavaan to recognize the nestedness of the models.

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am comparing two CFA models with categorical DV's, of the following form:

2factormodel <- 'f1a =~ item1 + item2 + item3
                        f1b =~ item4 + item5 + item6
                        f2 =~ item7 + item8 + item9

                        f1a ~~ 1 * f1b
                        f1a ~~ f2
                        f1b ~~ equal("f1a~~f2") * f2'

3factormodel <- 'f1a =~ item1 + item2 + item3
                        f1b =~ item4 + item5 + item6
                        f2 =~ item7 + item8 + item9'

When comparing the model fits using the anova function, I receive the following error:

Error in lav_func_jacobian_complex(func = af, x = m1@Fit@x) :
  function does not support non-numeric (complex) argument

I found this odd, since I subsequently compared the models using MPlus (with the DIFFTEST function), and this did provide me with sensible output.

Does anyone know why this occurs in Lavaan?

Thanks!

Are you using blavaan?  DIC is a Bayesian analog of AIC.  If you are using MLE, then look at AIC. If you are using blavaan for Bayesian estimation, you can get DIC and WAIC using the fitMeasures() function.

messages.subject_clean: error import data from SPSS to R
messages.body_plain:
> I check my data in SPSS and i have integers numbers and dont' have missings....  But... when i import my data to R reports a different number, for example decimal numbers.  I don't know if that " error" is a bug or If I'am doing something wrong with R or SPSS.

SPSS does not have a special "integer" type, just "Scale" (i.e., floating-point numbers -- in R this is equivalent to the "numeric" class).  If you only see integers in the SPSS Data Viewer, then that is just the choice for the display.  You can change the number of displayed decimal points in Variable View to check whether there are non-integer numbers in the SPSS data that need to be corrected.

In R, if you need a variable to be "integer" rather than floating-point "numeric", you can change it:

> myData$myVariable <- as.integer(myData$myVariable)

But that will just drop any decimal values (i.e., round down).  So you should correct those values in R or SPSS if they need to be corrected.

Terry

There is nothing wrong with estimating residual correlations.  If you actually expect the visual-speed correlation to be completely accounted for by their correlations with textual, then you can test that assumption by fixing the residual variance to zero.  See the lavaan tutorial pages for how to specify covariance parameters

> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html

and how to fix a parameter to a specific value (in your case, 0)

> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax2.html

messages.body_plain:
> Error in lav_func_jacobian_complex(func = af, x = m1@Fit@x) :
>   function does not support non-numeric (complex) argument

This might have something to do with the crazy math need to calculate chi-squared difference tests with ordered outcomes, combined with using a nonlinear equality constraint.  Instead of using the equal()* operator, try simply giving the 2 correlations the same label.

2factormodel <- 'f1a =~ item1 + item2 + item3
                 f1b =~ item4 + item5 + item6
                 f2 =~ item7 + item8 + item9

                 f1a ~~ 1*f1b

                 f1a ~~ Cov1*f2
                 f1b ~~ Cov1*f2 '

I think this method handles the equality constraint in a simpler way.  Compare Approaches 1 and 2 (I think using the equal()* operator is the equivalent of Approach 2): http://lavaan.ugent.be/notes/lavaan_eq_constraints.pdf

So using labels might work... worth a try.

Terry

Hi Henriette,

I use this example to test the multiple imputation for categorical items and it seems to work well. Can you check are there any differences between yours and me?

popModel <- "
f1 =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 + 0.7*y3 + 0.7*y4
f1 ~~ 1*f1
y1 | 0.5*t1
y2 | 0.25*t1
y3 | 0*t1
y4 | -0.5*t1
"

analyzeModel <- "
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
"

dat <- simulateData(popModel, sample.nobs  = 200L)
miss.pat <- matrix(as.logical(rbinom(prod(dim(dat)), 1, 0.2)), nrow(dat), ncol(dat))
dat[miss.pat] <- NA
out5 <- cfa.mi(analyzeModel, data=dat, ordered=paste0("y", 1:4), m = 3, miArgs=list(ords = c("y1", "y2", "y3", "y4")))
summary(out5)
inspect(out5, "fit")
inspect(out5, "impute")

Best,
Sunthud

> Terry

2016-02-01 11:28 GMT-03:00 Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com>:

> loadfit and mIC[["fit.loadings"]] have the same df, but I'm not sure that they are equivalent models (if they were, the chi-squared would be the same).  You say you read through Sunthud's lavaan scripts at the link you provided -- paying attention to those equality constraints tells you exactly how those models (and therefore, the output of measurementInvarianceCat) differ from the models you fit when you use the group.equal argument.  Your lavaan model syntax places no constraints on the thresholds whatsoever, whereas the method Sunthud (based on Millsap & Yun-Tein, 2004) does place equality constraints on the first threshold of each indicator, as well as the second threshold of the first indicator of each construct (i.e., u1 and u5) -- even in the configural model.  This enables the estimation not only of factor means in the second group, but also residual variances of each indicator's underlying latent response in the second group.  When you specify group.equal = "loadings", you did not freely estimate the residual variances, so your model-implied covariance matrix was different than the one implied by the model using semTools -- you can compare them directly:
>
> > lavInspect(loadfit, "cov.ov")
> > lavInspect(mIC[["fit.loadings"]], "cov.ov")
>
> This is what makes categorical CFA so much less intuitive than CFA with continuous indicators.  The thresholds affect not only mean-structure parameters but also covariance structure parameters.  For example
> If an indicator's latent response has a higher mean in group 2, that would manifest as a negative shift in the thresholds, but I think the distance between thresholds would stay the same (or proportionally equal, if the variances differed)
> If an indicator's latent response has a higher variance in group 2, that would manifest as a change in the distance between thresholds
> If you only have 1 threshold (binary indicator), then you cannot disentangle group-differences in means from group-differences in variances -- both would manifest as a difference in thresholds.  That is why you can't test weak and strong invariance separately with binary indicators.
>
> Anyway, the reason you have the same df using the 2 methods is that the 8 freely estimated residual variances are compensated by the 8 equality constraints on the first thresholds, and the 2 free factor means in group 2 are compensated by the 2 additional equality constraints on the second thresholds of u1 and u5.  So the number of estimated parameters is the same, but the models are not equivalent.
>
> And this is not a case of one method being wrong whereas the other is correct.  They are just 2 different methods, so you just need to pick one.  The Millsap & Yun-Tein (2004) method has more theoretical support because their publication was very thorough, but the point of their article was to delineate minimum identification constraints while being able to compare latent means and variances (the whole point of testing invariance).  They did not set out to make an exhaustive list of all possible ways to test measurement invariance with categorical indicators.
>
> Terry
>

Here is the code I used to test your model. It still works.

popmodel<-'A2~0.5*B1
 B2~0.3*A1+0.5*B1
 A1~~0.2*B1
 A2~~0.2*B2'

CLmodel<-'A2~B1
 B2~A1+B1
 A1~~B1
 A2~~B2'

dat <- simulateData(popmodel, sample.nobs = 200)
dat[matrix(as.logical(rbinom(200*4, 1, 0.1)), 200, 4)] <- NA

library(mice)
imp <- mice(dat, m=5)
mice.imp <- NULL
for(i in 1:5) mice.imp[[i]] <- complete(imp,action=i,include=FALSE)

library(semTools)
out <- runMI(CLmodel, data=mice.imp, chi="all",fun="sem")

Here is the code I used to test your model. It still works.

popmodel<-'A2~0.5*B1
 B2~0.3*A1+0.5*B1
 A1~~0.2*B1
 A2~~0.2*B2'

CLmodel<-'A2~B1
 B2~A1+B1
 A1~~B1
 A2~~B2'

dat <- simulateData(popmodel,

messages.body_plain:
My recommendation would be to check the imputations. I know mice says that with 5 iterations it usually converges, but you have to check it. Remember that mices runs as many iterations you tell it, it doesnt stop when the imputations have converged.

Sunthud's example shows that simulated well behave data works fine, but real data rarely behaves like that.

messages.subject: Re: assign bootstrap sample weights in boostrapLavaan?
messages.subject_clean: assign bootstrap sample weights in boostrapLavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Have you read http://amstat.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1988.10478591?
This might help, too:
http://web.missouri.edu/~kolenikovs/talks/svy_bstrap_ce_course.pdf
(pops us when you google Rao and Wu 1988 bootstrap; no self-promotion
whatsoever :) ). tl;dr: there are complications if you have complex
survey samples that go beyond just sticking weights somewhere. Even if
this works in terms of producing *something* in the output, the
numbers could be, as you put it, "wonky".

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)
-- Principal Survey Scientist, Abt SRBI
-- Education Officer, Survey Research Methods Section of the American
Statistical Association
-- Opinions stated in this email are mine only, and do not reflect the
position of my employer
-- http://stas.kolenikov.name

On Tue, Feb 9, 2016 at 4:12 PM, Tyler Scott
<tyler.and...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello,
>     Forgive me if I am simply overlooking an obvious reason why this would
> not work (or would produce wonky results), but is there any reason why it
> would be problematic for me to modify the boostrapLavaan code to assign
> sampling probabilities in the call to sample() within boostrapLavaan()?. For
> instance, modifying:
>
> ###Original
>
> fn <- function(b) {
> if(type == "bollen.stine" || type == "ordinary" || type == "yuan") {
> # take a bootstrap sample for each group
> for(g in 1:lavsamplestats@ngroups) {
> stopifnot(lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]] > 1L)
> boot.idx <- sample(x=lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]],
> size=lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]], replace=TRUE)
> dataX[[g]] <- dataX[[g]][boot.idx,,drop=FALSE]
> if(!is.null(dataeXo[[g]]))
> dataeXo[[g]] <- dataeXo[[g]][boot.idx,,drop=FALSE]
> }
> } else { # parametric!
> for(g in 1:lavsamplestats@ngroups) {
> dataX[[g]] <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]],
> Sigma = Sigma.hat[[g]],
> mu = Mu.hat[[g]])
> }
> }
>
>
> to be:
>
> ###MODIFIED
>
> fn <- function(b) {
> if(type == "bollen.stine" || type == "ordinary" || type == "yuan") {
> # take a bootstrap sample for each group
> for(g in 1:lavsamplestats@ngroups) {
> stopifnot(lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]] > 1L)
> boot.idx <- sample(x=lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]],
> size=lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]], replace=TRUE,prob = VECTOR.OF.PROBABILITIES)
> dataX[[g]] <- dataX[[g]][boot.idx,,drop=FALSE]
> if(!is.null(dataeXo[[g]]))
> dataeXo[[g]] <- dataeXo[[g]][boot.idx,,drop=FALSE]
> }
> } else { # parametric!
> for(g in 1:lavsamplestats@ngroups) {
> dataX[[g]] <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = lavsamplestats@nobs[[g]],
> Sigma = Sigma.hat[[g]],
> mu = Mu.hat[[g]])
> }
> }
>
> Thanks in advance for the input.
>
> -tyler
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: lisrel in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: lisrel in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> I want to get a result like lisrel software in lavaan. What do I do ?

Do you mean you want to view the output in the form of parameter matrices?  Use the lavInspect() function to view the point and SE estimates in their respective matrices:

> example(sem)
> lavInspect(fit, "coef")
> lavInspect(fit, "se")

If you want the same numerical solution as LISREL provides when fitting equivalent models in both programs, you can try requesting mimic = "lisrel" when you call lavaan (or cfa or sem), but that currently just gets reset to mimic = "EQS".  I wouldn't expect that to change anytime soon -- I am pretty sure there is more interest among lavaan users for new features than for mimicking the software of a previous generation of researchers (no disrespect for Jöreskog or LISREL-users intended).

Terry

messages.subject: Re: CFA and bootstrap
messages.subject_clean: CFA and bootstrap
messages.body_plain:
The bootstrap method is resampling with replacement from the original
data. So yes, you do need the raw data for the bootstrap to make any
sense. Then within each bootstrap replicate, you could compute your
correlation matrix and feed it to lavaan. If you are just using
somebody else's data, then you are stuck. If you are using your own
data, you should supply the data. From how your correlation matrix
looks like, though, it appears that you are simulating a rather
difficult scenario with highly correlated factors and low unique
factor variances... as if you are trying to break lavaan down :). If
you want to see how the bootstrap works for a correlation matrix like
that, you would want to simulate a data set out of this matrix, e.g.
as mvnorm(n=whatever,Sigma=mat.1,mu=rep(0,6) ).

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have the following cross-lagged panel model, in which I want to control for 3 covariates (meds + drugs + can_premor) in the regression paths for both outcomes (can_Y2 and relapse_Y2).

I ran the following model:

     M1 <- '

    # Lagged path

      can_Y2 ~ relapse_Y1

      relapse_Y2 ~ can_Y1

    # Autoregressive path

      can_Y2 ~ can_Y1

      relapse_Y2 ~ relapse_Y1

    # Covariates

      can_Y2 ~ meds + drugs + can_premor

      relapse_Y2 ~ meds + drugs + can_premor'

Fit measures:

chisq          pvalue         cfi               tli                rmsea

   0                NA              1               1                0

Based on the fit estimates, this model doesn’t seem appropriate to me. I also ran one model that included the covariates only for one of the main outcomes and this model seem to fit better:

   M2 <- '

    # Lagged path

      can_Y2 ~ relapse_Y1

      relapse_Y2 ~ can_Y1

    # Autoregressive path

      can_Y2 ~ can_Y1

      relapse_Y2 ~ relapse_Y1

    # Covariates

      relapse_Y2 ~ meds + drugs + can_premor'

Fit measures:

chisq          pvalue         cfi               tli                rmsea

1.750          0.626          1.000          1.054          0.000

The two models give me the same regression estimates for the variables included, but the model fits are different. So I was wondering whether I can I include my covariates only in one of the regression paths or am I missing something in my initial models (M1)?

Any advice in this regard would be much appreciated!

Kind regards,

Tabea

Dear all,

I have the following cross-lagged panel model, in which I want to control for 3 covariates (meds + drugs + can_premor) in the regression paths for both outcomes (can_Y2 and relapse_Y2).

I

messages.subject: Re: Regression results from SEM and fit measures
messages.subject_clean: Regression results from SEM and fit measures
messages.body_plain:
> Fit measures:
>
> chisq          pvalue         cfi               tli                rmsea
>
>    0                NA              1               1                0
>
>
>
> Based on the fit estimates, this model doesn’t seem appropriate to me.

The fit measures indicator your model fits perfectly, and the p value is missing because you have no degrees of freedom.  This is because your model is saturated (you are estimating as many covariance-structure parameters as you have observed (co)variances).

> I also ran one model that included the covariates only for one of the main outcomes and this model seem to fit better:

> Fit measures:

> chisq          pvalue         cfi               tli                rmsea
>
> 1.750          0.626          1.000          1.054          0.000

No, the model fits worse, because the chi-squared is now greater than zero.  But the p value says the fit is not significantly worse, and the other fit indices say your model still fits approximately the same (i.e., as well as can be expected).  The reason this model has 3 df is because you are estimating the effects of 3 covariates on relapse_Y2, but you omit those paths (i.e., fix them to zero) for can_Y2.

> The two models give me the same regression estimates for the variables included, but the model fits are different.

If all you are interested in are the regression estimates for the sake of making predictions, then it is not necessary to be concerned with model fit.  These fit measures are for using the data to test whether your theory is compatible with what you observe.  If you have a theory that suggests certain paths can be constrained to zero, then adding those constraints will make your model over-identified instead of just-identified.  You can find more information in path analysis chapters of introductory SEM textbooks -- the folks on SEMNET can volunteer good suggestions, if you don't already have one.  SEMNET  <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>is a great resource for general questions about SEM.

Regarding lavaan specifically, it is worth noting that you are probably estimating more parameters than you explicitly put in your model syntax.  If you use the sem() function, then you are automatically estimating the residual covariance among the Y2 variables.  In the lavaan() function, this is turned of (auto.cov.y = FALSE), but you can set it to TRUE to get the same results as from sem(), but there is no real reason to fix that residual covariance to zero -- saying your set of predictors completely explains the relationship between the two Y2 variables is a pretty big claim.  You can always see which parameters are being freely estimated by checking the parameter table:

> example(cfa)
> parTable(fit)

or by checking which elements of each parameter matrix are free (the ones that are not 0):

> lavInspect(fit, "free")

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> package ‘lavaan’ is not available (for R version 3.0.2)

We are now in R version 3.2.3, so you should try to update R.  Your current version is from 2013.

> https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/old/

I think the last version of lavaan built for R 3.0 was 0.5-16.  You can always find old versions by clicking on the link to "Old sources" when you look up the package description on CRAN.

> https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/lavaan/

If you can't build (or find a built copy of) R 3.2 for Ubuntu, then you can download the source code for lavaan 0.5-16 from the archive linked above, then install it directly from the source.

> install.packages("PATH TO YOUR lavaan FILE", type = "source", repos = NULL)

You could also install it by using the appropriate URL linking to the source code you want:

> install.packages("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/lavaan/lavaan_0.5-16.tar.gz",
>                  type = "source", repos = NULL)

Feel free to try lavaan 0.5-19 first, then work your way back in time if that doesn't work.  I'm not sure when your incompatibility actually began.  But the ideal situation is updating R, because many updates to lavaan have been made since 2013.

Dear Terry,

Thank you very much indeed for your very helpful answer – that made a lot of sense to me! I now ran the saturated model and then one model in which I dropped all paths that were not significant in the initial one.

I have one more question, which already came up in this group but I haven’t yet managed to solve it: When I include the correlation term (can_Y1 ~~ relapse_Y1),

    # Autoregressive path

      can_Y2 ~ can_Y1

    # Correlation

I get the following error message:

Error in vnames(FLAT, type = "ov.x", ov.x.fatal = TRUE) :

  lavaan ERROR: model syntax contains variance/covariance/intercept formulas

  involving (an) exogenous variable(s): [relapse_Y1 can_Y1];

  Please remove them and try again.

I can’t use fixed.x=FALSE, since I am using estimator="WLSMV".

I was just wondering whether there is a way of including the correlation between can_Y1 and relapse_Y1 in the model?

Many thanks again for your advice.

Kind regards,

Tabea

On Thursday, February 18, 2016 at 8:48:22 AM UTC, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > Fit measures:
> >
> > chisq          pvalue         cfi               tli                rmsea
> >
> >    0                NA              1               1                0
> >
> >
> >
> > Based on the fit estimates, this model doesn’t seem appropriate to me.
>
> The fit measures indicator your model fits perfectly, and the p value is missing because you have no degrees of freedom.  This is because your model is saturated (you are estimating as many covariance-structure parameters as you have observed (co)variances).
>
> > I also ran one model that included the covariates only for one of the main outcomes and this model seem to fit better:
> >
> > Fit measures:
> >
> > chisq          pvalue         cfi               tli                rmsea
> >
> > 1.750          0.626          1.000          1.054          0.000
>
> No, the model fits worse, because the chi-squared is now greater than zero.  But the p value says the fit is not significantly worse, and the other fit indices say your model still fits approximately the same (i.e., as well as can be expected).  The reason this model has 3 df is because you are estimating the effects of 3 covariates on relapse_Y2, but you omit those paths (i.e., fix them to zero) for can_Y2.
>
> > The two models give me the same regression estimates for the variables included, but the model fits are different.
>
> If all you are interested in are the regression estimates for the sake of making predictions, then it is not necessary to be concerned with model fit.  These fit measures are for using the data to test whether your theory is compatible with what you observe.  If you have a theory that suggests certain paths can be constrained to zero, then adding those constraints will make your model over-identified instead of just-identified.  You can find more information in path analysis chapters of introductory SEM textbooks -- the folks on SEMNET can volunteer good suggestions, if you don't already have one.  SEMNET  <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>is a great resource for general questions about SEM.
>
> Regarding lavaan specifically, it is worth noting that you are probably estimating more parameters than you explicitly put in your model syntax.  If you use the sem() function, then you are automatically estimating the residual covariance among the Y2 variables.  In the lavaan() function, this is turned of (auto.cov.y = FALSE), but you can set it to TRUE to get the same results as from sem(), but there is no real reason to fix that residual covariance to zero -- saying your set of predictors completely explains the relationship between the two Y2 variables is a pretty big claim.  You can always see which parameters are being freely estimated by checking the parameter table:
>
> > example(cfa)
> > parTable(fit)
>
> or by checking which elements of each parameter matrix are free (the ones that are not 0):
>
> > lavInspect(fit, "free")
>
> Terry
>

messages.body_plain:
Both of the warning messages are tied to the parameter estimates listed under "Variances" in the output.  Note that the (residual) variance estimates for several of your observed variables are negative.  Even one negative variance will typically make the matrix of residual covariances be not positive definite,so both messages are really telling you about the same thing.
    There is a conflict in your syntax.  You specify that the first loading for each factor must be fixed at 1, as in:

                     social_well_being =~ 1*faces_total_sa + faces_total_sc

.  This constrains the variance of the associated factor to be equal to variance(y) - residual variance(y), where y is the observed variable whose loading is fixed to 1. But you also specify that the variance of each factor must be equal to 1, as in:
                     social_well_being ~~ 1*social_well_being
This is a conflict.  .Where the factor is dependent on another factor, this specification affects the residual variance of the factor, ratehr than the total variance, but it is still likely to be inconfict with the loading-fixed-to-1 specification.
     My advice is to delete the lines of code where you set factor variances (or residual variances) to 1:

                     # factor variances
                     social_well_being ~~ 1*social_well_being
                     optimism ~~ 1*optimism
                     stress_in_life ~~ 1*stress_in_life
                     mental_health ~~ 1*mental_health

Comment out those lines (or delete them), and I believe this particular issue will be removed.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Chris--
What function are you using?  If you are using the lavaan function, then you would nee to fix residual variances for the observed variables that are single indicators for their factors (the indicators for optimism, stress in life and mental health).  If you were using the sem function, then by default these residual variances would be fixed to 0--though you could set them to different values.  With the lavaan function, I can see how both fixing first loadings and fixing factor variances could conceal the identification problem.  But if you just switch to the sem function, I believe that will eliminate the warning about an identification problem.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
> I'm trying to fit a growth model to my data and am getting these warnings:

> Warning messages:
> 1: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
>   lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
> 2: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
>   lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.
>

> As far as I can see my data are pretty straight forward so I'm puzzled why I'm getting these warnings.

The example data you posted only had a negative variance for the intercept, although the SE was more than 3 times larger, so you can't reject the null hypothesis that the intercept variance is nonnegative in the population.  Did you simulate the data to have a substantial variance of intercepts?  Was this the same parameter estimate that was causing the error with your real data?

Here is an enlightening article on Heywood cases:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138

Essentially, when population values are close to natural boundaries, sampling error alone could (possibly) be responsible for finite-sample estimates to be distributed across the boundary.  To test the null hypothesis that the population variance is nonnegative, you should use a bootstrap CI by setting lavaan(..., se = "bootstrap") and parameterEstimates(..., boot.ci.type = "bca.simple"), or at least use robust SEs by setting lavaan(..., se = "robust.huber.white").

Terry

> I can’t use fixed.x=FALSE, since I am using estimator="WLSMV".
>
>
>
> I was just wondering whether there is a way of including the correlation between can_Y1 and relapse_Y1 in the model?

You don't need to include it in the model.  They are exogenous, so their correlation is assumed to be a known value (the sample correlation).  The fact that they aren't estimated does not mean that the correlation is fixed to zero.  It is just that their effects are partialed out.  The WLS criterion is effectively minimizing the error variance of the endogenous variables only (just like in regular regression, except OLS regression is unweighted least squares).

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Chris--
In your new model syntax, the lines:

                     # factor covariances
                     faces_total_sa ~~ faces_total_sc
                     faces_total_sa ~~ les_total_s'

refer to observed variables, not factors. In fact, since these variables are dependent on factors, these lines refer to the residual variances of these observed variables.   Your ability to allow free residual covariances is limited by the factor model that you are attempting to estimate. The only common factors in your model are social well being, optimism, stress in life and mental health. Some of the covariances or residual covariances among these common factors are free by default. Some cannot be freed without wrecking the regression relationships that you are trying to estimate.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terry,

Thanks a lot for your response.

This is the same error I get for my real data.

In my simulated data I meant for all factors (each genotype sex combination) to have the same intercept but differing slopes. Perhaps that the proximity of the intercept variance to zero is what's causing this - as you suggest.

However running either:
fit <- growth(model, data=sim.df.tab, se = "bootstrap")

or
fit <- growth(model, data=sim.df.tab, se = "robust.huber.white")

I still get the same warnings:

Warning messages:
1: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
2: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.

Thanks a lot,
rubi

On Tuesday, February 23, 2016 at 3:39:42 AM UTC-5, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I'm trying to fit a growth model to my data and am getting these warnings:
> > Warning messages:
> > 1: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
> >   lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
> > 2: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
> >   lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.
> >
> >
> > As far as I can see my data are pretty straight forward so I'm puzzled why I'm getting these warnings.
>
> The example data you posted only had a negative variance for the intercept, although the SE was more than 3 times larger, so you can't reject the null hypothesis that the intercept variance is nonnegative in the population.  Did you simulate the data to have a substantial variance of intercepts?  Was this the same parameter estimate that was causing the error with your real data?
>
> Here is an enlightening article on Heywood cases:
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138
>
> Essentially, when population values are close to natural boundaries, sampling error alone could (possibly) be responsible for finite-sample estimates to be distributed across the boundary.  To test the null hypothesis that the population variance is nonnegative, you should use a bootstrap CI by setting lavaan(..., se = "bootstrap") and parameterEstimates(..., boot.ci.type = "bca.simple"), or at least use robust SEs by setting lavaan(..., se = "robust.huber.white").
>
> Terry
>

Rubi,

  Let me add a little to what Terry wrote.  His suggestion was to use the robust or bootstrap standard errors to test whether your negative variance was within sampling error of zero.  You should get the same estimates, the only difference should be the method used to compute the standard errors.

  Another possibility, aside from sampling error, is that the negative variance reflects model misspecification.  Sometimes, a negative variance compensates for another aspect of a model implying excessive variance or covariance.  I notice that you simulated your data with a genotype by gender interaction in determining the slope.  For example, for females WT and PD have the same slope, but not for males, if I follow your code correctly.  However, your model contains only main effects for genotype and gender.  This misspecification might (and this is only a conjecture) explain your negative variance.

Keith

John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

On Tuesday, February 23, 2016 at 8:44:54 AM UTC, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > I can’t use fixed.x=FALSE, since I am using estimator="WLSMV".
> >
> >
> >
> > I was just wondering whether there is a way of including the correlation between can_Y1 and relapse_Y1 in the model?
>
> You don't need to include it in the model.  They are exogenous, so their correlation is assumed to be a known value (the sample correlation).  The fact that they aren't estimated does not mean that the correlation is fixed to zero.  It is just that their effects are partialed out.  The WLS criterion is effectively minimizing the error variance of the endogenous variables only (just like in regular regression, except OLS regression is unweighted least squares).
>
> Terry

messages.body_plain:
The difference is not lavaan vs other factor-based SEM software, but factor-based SEM vs regression. In regression's F test, the DF in the numerator increase as free parameters are added, but in factor-based SEM's chi-square statistic, DF decline as free parameters are added.  In either technique, imposing an equality constraint reduces the number of free parameters.
